bib.title: Siren's Song in the AI Ocean: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models

read.skipped: Reference list (from about char 97874 to end) skimmed only for lineage; body, all tables, limitations and conclusion read in full. There is no appendix.

question: How should hallucination in large language models be defined, evaluated, explained and mitigated across the LLM life cycle?
contributions: A three-way taxonomy of LLM hallucination: input-conflicting, context-conflicting, fact-conflicting
A review of evaluation benchmarks (generation vs discrimination) and metrics (human, model-based, rule-based)
An analysis of four sources of hallucination and of mitigation at pre-training, SFT, RLHF and inference
Open directions: reliable evaluation, multilingual, multimodal, model editing, attack/defense, reasoning models

limits: The survey reports no experiments of its own; the Table 6 scores are compiled with no source, prompt, model version or date, so they are not comparable across columns.
Automatic metrics for generation-style benchmarks do not align well with human annotation, and their reliability varies across domains and generator models (Sec 6).
How discrimination performance relates to generation performance is unknown (Sec 6).
Coverage is mostly English and mostly fact-conflicting hallucination; the authors say they focus there.
The authors treat all unverifiable content as fact-conflicting hallucination and concede this is contested.
Logit-based uncertainty does not work with closed APIs; verbalized confidence is over-confident; no settled way to measure consistency across samples.
Text refers to Table 4 for the external-knowledge summary, but the table is Table 11 (cross-reference error in the source).
The paper's own benchmark list is dated by 2023 to 2024 work; reasoning models are covered in only one short paragraph.
practices: Evaluate fact-conflicting hallucination in both formats, generation (TruthfulQA, FActScore, SimpleQA) and discrimination (HaluEval, FACTOR), because they test different abilities (Sec 3.1).
Use human evaluation as the reliable reference and validate any automatic metric against it (Sec 3.2).
Use model-based judges (GPT-judge, FActScore with a retriever plus LLM, AlignScore) as cheaper proxies for human labels, and check their agreement with human labels (Sec 3.2).
Prefer a mix of human and fully automatic benchmark construction: human review for quality, automatic pipelines for timely updates (Sec 3.1).
Curate pre-training data by filtering and up-sampling credible sources such as Wikipedia (Sec 5.1).
Curate SFT data by hand or with LLM filters, and inspect synthetic SFT data such as Alpaca for hallucinated answers (Sec 5.2).
Add honest 'I don't know' samples to SFT data, but expect weak out-of-distribution generalisation (Sec 5.2.2).
Prefer honesty-oriented RL with a reward that penalises confident wrong answers over honesty-oriented SFT, and watch for over-conservatism (Sec 5.3).
At inference, prefer greedy or factual-nucleus decoding over plain top-p for factual tasks (Sec 5.4.1).
Ground answers in retrieved evidence (generation-time supplement) or correct them after the fact with a fixer (post-hoc correction) (Sec 5.4.2).
Estimate uncertainty with logit-based, verbalized or consistency-based methods, and prefer consistency-based ones for black-box APIs (Sec 5.4.3).
Use multi-agent debate or multi-persona prompting to reduce hallucination (Sec 5.4.4).
Instruct models in the system prompt not to share false information, and use chain-of-thought with the caveat that reasoning steps can themselves hallucinate (Sec 5.4.5).

terms.definition: LLMs generate content that deviates from the source input provided by users
LLMs generate content that conflicts with previously generated information by itself
LLMs generate content that is either inconsistent with established world knowledge or cannot be verified by it
Treats hallucination as a generation characteristic and evaluates the generated text
Tests whether the LLM can discriminate truthful statements from hallucinated ones
False statements with a high likelihood on the training distribution
LLMs generate responses that favor the user's perspective rather than correct or truthful answers
LLMs over-commit to early mistakes and prefer self-consistency over recovering from errors
Introducing honest samples, responses that admit incompetence, into the SFT data
A reward function designed to encourage LLMs to challenge the premise, express uncertainty and admit incapability
Measures uncertainty by token-level probability or entropy; needs model logits
Directly asks the LLM to express its uncertainty, for example a 0 to 100 confidence score
Assumes LLMs give logically inconsistent responses to the same question when indecisive and hallucinating
Two ways to use retrieved knowledge: concatenate it with the query before generation, or have an auxiliary fixer rectify the output afterwards

figures.caption: The overview structure of this paper: We initially categorize LLM hallucinations into three distinct types and then introduce corresponding evaluation benchmarks. Subsequently, we explore the source of hallucinations and discuss mitigation strategies throughout the life cycle of LLMs (pre-training, SFT, RLHF, inference).
figures.why: Maps hallucination sources to mitigation stage across the LLM life cycle.
